# 6.11 Inflation and Real Returns

Planning in real returns; how assets and liabilities protect against inflation; I bonds; matching retirement spending with TIPS; personal inflation and the CPI.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/6.11-key.md

A household's goals are about buying things in the future: a home, education, life in retirement. Their prices rise with inflation, so planning should use real returns (real interest rate), not nominal ones.

## Planning in real terms

People tend to think in nominal amounts: a 3% raise feels like getting richer even if prices also rose 3%. This tendency is called **money illusion**. The way to avoid it in household planning is to state every goal in today's purchasing power, use real rates of return after inflation, and read the results in today's purchasing power too. Capital market assumptions (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/) are usually given as real returns.

Planning must also separate incomes and expenses that adjust with inflation from those that do not: Social Security adjusts for inflation; most private pensions and ordinary annuities are fixed nominal amounts; and the payment on a fixed-rate mortgage is a fixed nominal amount too.

## Which assets protect against inflation

Assets protect against inflation in different ways, and one must distinguish expected from unexpected inflation, and the short run from the long run:

- Cash and Treasury bills: their rates adjust to expected inflation and keep up in the short run, but their real return is often near 0.
- Nominal bonds: unexpected inflation lowers their real value, more so the longer the maturity (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/).
- Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS): the principal adjusts with the CPI, guaranteeing a real return if held to maturity (Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/#tips).
- The **I bond** (Series I savings bond): a savings bond issued by the US Treasury whose rate combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate reset every six months from the CPI. I bonds do not trade in a market; they can be redeemed at their accrued value, so their nominal value never falls; they must be held at least 1 year, and redeeming within 5 years forfeits the last 3 months of interest; each person can buy at most 10,000 dollars a year; interest is taxed federally only at redemption and is exempt from state tax. I bonds bought from November 2026 to April 2027 have a fixed rate of 1.40% and a composite rate of 5.51%.
- Stocks: companies' revenues and assets rise with prices, so stocks keep up with inflation in the long run, but in the short run unexpected inflation often comes with rising rates and falling valuations (Lesson 2.8, "Business Cycles and Asset Prices" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-8-business-cycle-asset-prices/#stock-bond).
- Commodities and real estate: somewhat positively related to inflation (Lesson 5.5, "Alternative Assets" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/5-5-alternative-assets/), but very volatile themselves.
- Fixed-rate liabilities: inflation lightens their real burden, a hedge for the borrower (Lesson 6.6, "The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-6-household-balance-sheet/#debt).

## Matching retirement spending with TIPS

Most spending in retirement rises with prices; it is a real liability. Matching it with real assets carries the least risk: for example a ladder of TIPS with different maturities, one maturing each year to provide that year's real spending (Exercises Question 2). This is the same idea as immunization, matching liabilities by duration (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/#immunization), with a real liability in place of a nominal one. Lesson 6.12, "Goals-Based Investing" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-12-goals-based-investing/ extends this idea to all of a household's goals.

## Personal inflation

The CPI measures the average price change of a basket of goods and services bought by urban consumers (consumer price index), but every household spends differently. Retirees spend more on health care and housing, whose prices often rise faster than average; households with mortgages are affected differently by rising home prices than renters are. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an experimental index weighted by the spending of households aged 62 and over (CPI-E). Social Security is adjusted by the CPI-W; the 2026 adjustment was 2.8%.

> **Check question C5**
> 
> If the CPI rose 2.8% over a year, then every retiree's cost of living rose by about 2.8% that year.
> 
> (True or false)
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

## Summary

- Plan in today's purchasing power and real returns, avoiding money illusion; separate incomes and expenses that adjust with inflation from those that do not.
- Nominal bonds suffer from unexpected inflation; TIPS and I bonds protect real value; stocks keep up with inflation in the long run but not necessarily in the short run; fixed-rate liabilities favor the borrower.
- Retirement spending is a real liability that a TIPS ladder can match.
- Personal inflation can differ from the CPI, especially for retirees.

## Exercises

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

A 35-year-old investor sees an online calculator saying: "To retire at 65, you need 2 million dollars." The calculator assumes 3% inflation and a 7% nominal return.
(a) What is 2 million dollars in 30 years worth in today's purchasing power (thousand dollars)? What real return corresponds to the 7% nominal return?
(b) He says: "At 4% a year, 2 million dollars gives 80,000 dollars a year, enough for my current 70,000 dollars a year of spending." Evaluate this statement, and say how to avoid this kind of mistake.

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

A 65-year-old retiree wants 40,000 dollars (in today's purchasing power) at the end of each of the next 10 years. TIPS at all maturities yield 1.8% real, and nominal Treasuries at all maturities yield 4.2%.
(a) How much does a TIPS ladder providing this spending cost today (thousand dollars)? How much does a nominal Treasury ladder paying a fixed 40,000 nominal dollars a year cost? With 3% inflation, how much would nominal Treasuries cost to pay the inflation-adjusted amounts $40 \times 1.03^t$?
(b) He says: "The nominal ladder costs only 320,000 dollars and TIPS 360,000, so obviously choose nominal." Evaluate this statement.

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

The I bond composite rate is $f + 2i + f \times i$, where $f$ is the fixed rate and $i$ the semiannual inflation rate. In November 2026: $f = 1.40\%$, $i = 2.04\%$.
(a) Compute the composite rate.
(b) A household has 50,000 dollars that may go toward a home down payment in 3 to 5 years. A friend suggests: "Put it all in I bonds: 5.51% and inflation protection, nothing beats it." Evaluate this suggestion. What limits and alternatives should be considered?

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

A household holds 300,000 dollars of intermediate and long nominal Treasuries (modified duration 7) and owes a 400,000 dollar 30-year fixed-rate mortgage whose modified duration, valued at market rates, is about 8. Suppose unexpected inflation raises rates at all maturities by 2 percentage points.
(a) Using the duration approximation (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/), roughly how much does the bonds' market value change? How much does the market value of the mortgage liability change? How much does the household's net worth change (thousand dollars)?
(b) They say: "Inflation is very bad for us, because our bonds will drop sharply." Evaluate this statement. What does this calculation leave out?
